AI Capex - Financing The Investment Cycle Implications of the Upcoming AI/Data Center Funding Surge The global data center and AI buildout will be an extraordinary and sustained capital markets event. Building out global data center and AI infrastructure and related power supplies could cost over \$5 trillion in our view, with at least one consultant calling for \$7 trillion of global AI-related capex. Funding that extraordinary growth will likely require participation from every public capital market as well as private credit, alternative capital providers and even government involvement. The question is not “which market will finance the AI-boom”. Rather, the question is “how will financings be structured to access every capital market.” The sheer scale of those investments has critical implications across the credit market landscape. Big picture, for various reasons public bond and syndicated loan market growth has slowed post-COVID recovery (shrunk in the case of High Yield Bonds). AI/Data Centers are likely to drive a re-acceleration of market growth. The scale of demand for compute remains astronomical, with actual growth somewhat constrained by physical limitations. Our base case estimates call for 122 GW of global data center infrastructure capacity installations from 2026-2030, at a rapidly accelerating rate. We have written in the past (US Credit Research: Data Center Deliberations: Credit Implications Of A Growing Mega-Trend) about data center growth being constrained by real estate, energy and power, water, commodity prices and capital. Thankfully, that remains true, else the potential funding needs would be even higher. Our colleagues in Asia produce an intriguing bottoms up unconstrained forecast based on semiconductor orders that implies growth of 144 GW globally through YE2028 - i.e.basically the same amount of growth in the next three years as we forecast over the next five years once factoring critical constraints. Power is the most important of those constraints. Current lead times for new natural gas turbines have ballooned to 3-4 years, and nuclear plants have historically taken 10+ years to build. Adding 150 GW of power in a timely manner is a remarkable challenge, particularly in light of grid upgrade requirements. Recent comments from certain power producers suggest some flexibility is possible from ramping up peakers more aggressively, but that has implications for retail prices. Balancing ultimate retail electricity prices (still stable as a percentage of income, at least in the US) is a politically important and sensitive aspect of managing the data center boom.
Funding curve manageable now, larger call on alternatives down the road. Annual data center funding needs in 2026 are on the order of \$700 billion, which could be entirely financed by hyperscaler cash flow and High Grade bond markets. However, 2030 funding needs are in excess of \$1.4 trillion, which will likely require funding contributions from all capital providing markets.
Hyperscaler cash flow will have to do an enormous amount of the heavy lifting. Hyperscalers are generating over \$700 billion of operating cash flow per annum, and reinvesting \~\$500 billion of that back into capex . Note that \~\$500 billion of reinvestment back into the collective businesses does not include \~\$250 billion of research and development spending per year. We are assuming approximately \$300 billion per year of hyperscaler capex reflects cash flow funded AI and data center capex (while AI is crowding out a lot of spending, its not crowding out all spending).
High Grade capital markets will look very different. We think High Grade markets could absorb \$300 billion of AI/data center related paper over the next year, and are assuming \$1.5 trillion of funding from High Grade bond markets over the next five years. AI/Data center capex-related sectors already represent 14.5% of the JULI Index, which is larger than the US Banks component of the index. Mathematically, if anything like our forecast plays out, AI/ Data Center related sectors could represent north of 20% of the market by 2030. Historically, lumpy issuance from select sectors is not “new” to High Grade. Recent examples like Healthcare (‘21-’24) and Telecom (‘16-’19) have been manageable and in both cases led to 15-20bp of underperformance from the impacted sector.
The securitization market is a natural home for data center funding, but... We expect the securitization markets to absorb \$30-\$40 billion per annum of data center risk, ramping up modestly over time. Critically, the securitization market is providing construction financing via fully amortizing structures, as opposed to permanent stable financings. That somewhat limits the footprint….perhaps for now.

There is capacity for meaningful data center funding from the Leveraged Finance markets, but the history of “the new largest sector” has been poor. We think the new issue market across Leveraged Finance could comfortably finance \$150 billion over the next five years, with the recent examples of Financials supportive of that number. However, the history of High Yield Telecom in the 1990s and Energy from 2010-2015 as both grew to become the largest sector in the marketplace at the time does at least deserve some consideration.
Potentially large call on alternative capital and governments to bring this to fruition. Private credit has become a key part of the leveraged finance ecosystem, and the sheer amount of dry powder (\~\$466 billion on an unleveraged basis today prior to any incremental fundraising) implies a meaningful role in filling the potential \~\$1.4 trillion funding gap in our analysis. There has been substantial focus on recent private deal structures (with the Beignet private to public structure particularly notable). The flexibility within private credit and alternative structures to better match cash flows and solve for ratings outcomes does argue for a role for private credit beyond just providing capital. Some might ask - where are the banks? We expect the banking system to continue to be an important source of temporary/ bridge capital, but financing long-term assets permanently with short-duration bank loans would be a material asset/liability mismatch. Government involvement has run the gamut from aggressively and publicly supportive in the US to a safety-focused regime in the EU. More aggressive financial support by governments is possible, particularly if/when national defense concerns around AI grow.
The path from here to there will not just be “up and to the right”. Our biggest fear would be a repeat of the telecom and fiber buildout experiences, where the revenue curve failed to materialize at a pace that justified continued investment. For now, commentary from large corporates suggests benefits are starting to be realized at scale. More interestingly, OpenAI just publicly commented that they have achieved a \$20 billion annualized revenue run-rate already. However, breakthroughs or accelerated efficiency gains - as people initially thought occurred with Deepseek - could drive an overcapacity/dark fiber situation. Big picture, to drive a 10% return on our modeled AI investments through 2030 would require \~\$650 billion of annual revenue into perpetuity, which is an astonishingly large number. But for context, that equates to 58bp of global GDP, or \$34.72/month from every current iPhone user, or \$180/ month from every Netflix subscriber. How that is apportioned between corporations, governments and consumers is, of course, a long-term debate. Regardless, even if everything works, there will be (continued) spectacular winners, and probably some equally spectacular losers as well given the amount of capital involved and winner takes all nature of portions of the AI ecosystem.

Scale of AI/Data Center Growth Is Daunting
Datacenter capacity is measured by its power draw, and historically in MWs, figures that have multiplied and are now discussed in GWs. While there are varying degrees of estimates of the installed base globally in the US, the prevailing consensus is that before AI the installed base was about 50 GWs globally, with about half in the US. As we show below, over the last 18-24 months, an inflection in construction activity has begun, and continued at a ferocious pace. Estimates have a range, but Vertiv, a leading DC Infra player, in November 2024 talked about 100 GWs being added globally between 2025 and 2029, while competitor Eaton presented a view in March of the installed base going from 21GW to 74-132GW, adding \~100 GW, but only in the US, and today they talk about a pipeline going from \$200 B at the beginning of the year to now something close to \$500 B. Our US funnel of land bank, permitting and announcements totals 320 GWs showing the degree of prep going on at a grass roots level, and finally, measuring what is needed using the silicon shipments expectations shows a 285 GW number globally. If we assume a stair step in activity merely looking at the spreadsheet, one could surmise that off the 2 GW added annually before this cycle, that doubled in 2024, and is likely doubling again in 2025, moving beyond 10 GWs in 2026. These numbers are hard to come by with accurate estimates, but the point is that the trajectory is accelerating, a dynamic reflected in the order books of major players as recently as 3Q, many of whom talked about 70%+ growth. The high level models below illustrate the runway here.
We show these estimates in the table and how they differ, categorizing them into the “high end” camp, which shows a CAGR of 25-30% in MW added from ‘24 to ‘28, the “mid range” estimates, a \~low 20% CAGR, and then “low end”, a \~mid teens % CAGR. Notably, the low end estimate has moved up from what was 10% a year ago, showing we are no longer early innings in the discovery process. For purposes of our funding needs analysis, we have used numbers consistent with mid-range growth scenarios to reflect physical constraints over the next five years.

Our bottom-up build of data center power demand, based on JPM estimates of AIrelated chip shipments and power requirements. The simplified high level analysis continues to show a staggering installations outlook, with a cumulative \~135 GWs of added power over the next five years, which we haircut by \~30% for potential efficiency gains and other constraints (land, power, availability, supply chain, etc) to come to a base case that still suggests \~100 GWs, a 25% CAGR driven by 30%+ for AI-related installs/TAM, resulting in a more than doubling of the installed base to 160 GWs. The unit growth estimate compares to VRT estimates for the data center market to grow 10- 13% on a blended basis, with 15-17% at hyperscale/colo and 4-6% at enterprise, with 100 GW added globally from 2023-2029 which looks conservative based on the model. We believe that downside could be the result of simply fewer units required for the degree of computing power being consumed, but this is a call on model efficiency and how effective business models will be and would have implications across the AI hardware chain, something less visible to us today. We set this against experts’ estimates as a sanity check, with our number coming out somewhere in between the most conservative estimates we have seen (IEA) and the most aggressive (Semianalysis). The outcome shows growth that is materially faster than the market outlooks provided by the major players here that stand in the \~LDD % range, and based on the hard forecasts of what we know today, the numbers show dramatic best in class growth versus other parts of the capital goods economy. There is of course lots to play out when it comes to technology progression, and we continue to view this model as illustrative, but one where low-end estimates from a year ago have started to converge towards the mid-range. As a check, we note that on a GPU weighted basis, Stargate highlighted they were adding 450k GPUs in their 1.2 GW facility in Abilene while nScale was adding 10k GPUs in their 240 MW facility, also in Texas. A key difference is that their estimate of installed base is higher, in the 90 GWs range in 2024 vs the 2024 base in the EE/MI model of 40 GW (source: Semianalysis). One reason for the difference is the 40 GW is just IT equipment. Also, Asia Tech team is using IEA as reference. IEA has a higher base and also accounts for PUE and utilization to come to a much higher number of installation. Overall, JPM Asia Tech team estimates a 27% CAGR of datacenter power installed base from FY25-28. Consequently, the datacenter power installed base will grow to 242GW by 2028 vs. 97GW in 2024 (based on IEA data), implying a 26% CAGR over the period vs. historical growth trends at 10-20%. This would translate into \~1,100TWh and comprise 3-4% of global electricity consumption (vs. 1.5% in 2024). Census PIP Data Center Data Shows Ongoing Strength The US Census breaks out data center spending as a category in its monthly Put in Place report. Here we can see a continued strong trajectory, one that supports the ongoing sequential increase in activity. Importantly, while some view data center spending as elevated, it is still ‘only’ 6% of non-res spending, although rapidly increasing. Indeed, manufacturing is >5x the amount of data center spend. That said, datacenter spend has been a key driver of private non-res construction spending over the past year, with private non-res ex-data center down -5% YTD versus -3.5% all-in, showing how exposure to this vertical is key to outperforming the current downturn in spending. Development Pipeline and Land Banks Are “AI-popping”
Our in-house proprietary data center funnel which tracks US related project announcements since Jan ‘23 is currently tracking 315 GW+, with \~165 GW added YTD. To provide context, our funnel was around \~130 GW at this time last year, and \~175 GW before DeepSeek news hit the market and called for the apocalypse of the AI build out. In our belief, what DeepSeek did at best was create more demand for inference which is evident from our DC funnel, which has grown by \~150 GW since then. That’s almost half the entire funnel. To put the numbers in context, the US installed base was 20 GW by year-end 2022, and most of our companies (ETN/VRT) have called out for further adds of \~100 GW in the next 5 years. With the current set of investments, announcements on new GW clusters coming up, and Utes budget accelerating, it’s hard to believe that the adds won’t exceed the companies’ estimates. Stepping back, we discuss in this section further details from our DC funnel and trends from these project buildouts - including areas where they are being built, increasing density and major players amongst other things. Announcements here include plan proposal, plan filing, rezoning request, plan/rezoning approval, land purchase, etc. and we made a best effort attempt to adjust for cancellations and to not duplicate filings. All in, this funnel consists of 600+ projects and we try to track their status in terms of whether the project is approved to proceed, funding raised, shovel hitting the ground or facility being topped out. We take out projects from our funnel if they have gone live, and that represents a very small % of the overall funnel.

Hyperscaler Cash Flow Is The Foundation Of Growth Capital
The hyperscalers are rapidly entering a new phase of balance sheet evolution as AI and Data Center capital investment accelerates toward \~\$450bn/year. While these companies continue to generate exceptional operating cash flow, sustained double-digit capex intensity is beginning to compress FCF conversion and could gradually shift funding dynamics. To date, most of this spending has been internally financed, but incremental debt issuance, lease financing, and off-balance sheet structures are likely to play a growing role as investment scales. We have already seen some of these firms turn to the bond market to finance the initial capex wave, with \$18bn issued by Oracle at the end of September, a \$30bn deal from Meta two weeks ago, and another \$24bn financed by Alphabet in the EUR and USD markets last week. In this context, we assess the cash flow capacity, capex and leverage trajectory, and potential issuance outlook for each major “hyperscaler” — Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle — and examine the long-term implications for their balance sheets, credit profiles, and bond market participation.
The hyperscalers collectively hold over \~\$350bn in liquid cash and investments and are expected to generate \~\$725bn of operating cash flow in 2026. Even so, substantial new debt supply is coming to the credit markets from these high-quality issuers, through both regular-way IG senior note issuance and likely private transactions similar to Meta’s Beignet Investor LLC. Alphabet, Meta, and Oracle have all shown a willingness to fund record capex with debt thus far. Alphabet set the tone in May with \~ \$12bn across nine tranches in EUR and USD markets, followed by another \~\$24bn across fourteen tranches last week. Meta recently completed a \$30bn US IG offering, the largest YTD, alongside the \$27.3bn privately placed Beignet Investor LLC note issued by Blue Owl for Meta’s Hyperion Data Center project. Within the group, Meta has led the shift toward a blend of public and private funding, a trend likely to spread in our view. Oracle also issued a \$18bn multi-tranche deal in late September, and we see continued issuance as unavoidable given its balance sheet constraints, negative FCF, and \$40bn+ in combined dividend and capex commitments over the next year. Amazon and Microsoft’s appetite for issuance remains a question mark, though both seem primed to pursue structures similar to Beignet’s. While credit quality across the sector remains solid, this wave of issuance adds meaningful supply to an IG market that had been expecting a slowdown. The impact has already shown up in spreads, as \$30bn of new AA- rated Meta bonds sent META spreads 20+bps wider across the curve, before rebounding some this week. Similarly, Oracle’s \$18bn new deal has widened by between \~30-40bps since issuance. Near-term performance in high-quality Tech may stay pressured by supply, but we expect investors to remain attracted to these names given, for the most part, strong credit profiles, solid underlying performance, and limited alternatives despite record capex and weaker FCF.

Microsoft Of all the companies discussed, we view Microsoft as the least inclined to rely on debt to fund capex. The firm has tapped the market only once in the past five years to refinance a portion of the Activision debt taken on during the merger. In fact, Microsoft even funded the entire \$75bn Activision acquisition with cash on hand and commercial paper access, which it repaid within a year, highlighting its recent aversion to leverage. In effect, Microsoft now functions as both strategic partner and capital backstop, providing ongoing access to hyperscale compute, distribution, and liquidity while OpenAI gains the latitude to diversify funding and infrastructure sources. Oracle As of F1Q26, Oracle had \$91bn of debt outstanding, including \$2bn in short-term commercial paper. On September 25th, the company issued \$18bn of new senior notes across six tranches with maturities ranging from five to forty years to fund refinancing needs and AI-related capex. The deal reportedly had an order book demand of \~\$88bn, though we interpret the strong demand for new Oracle debt as a reflection of the lack of direct AI-related debt in the IG market at the time as opposed to a reflection of Oracle’s credit quality. The transaction lifted total debt above \$100bn, making Oracle the most indebted IG-rated Technology issuer and the fifth-largest within IG TMT overall. Nearterm maturities are manageable, with only \$1bn due before calendar year-end, though \$5.75bn will come due in calendar 2026 and an additional \$5bn in 2027. These obligations, combined with ongoing capex and dividend funding needs, suggest Oracle will remain a regular and significant IG market issuer as it manages its balance sheet commitments. With traditional balance sheet capacity increasingly constrained by negative FCF and elevated leverage, Oracle will likely also turn to private credit and structured financing channels to bridge its AI investment needs. For Oracle, arrangements similar to those of Beignet Investor LLC and the recent Vantage Data Center loans (discussed below) would provide incremental liquidity while deferring pressure on traditional credit markets and avoiding further ratings deterioration. However, reliance on private lenders and structured facilities also underscores the tightening of conventional debt capacity and introduces new layers of counterparty and refinancing risk. Oracle’s mid-BBB ratings and Negative outlooks from S&P and Moody’s could pose a challenge for pursuing a Beignet-like structure, which is notched one rating below Meta’s parent rating, as the project-level debt would presumably start at a low-BBB rating with a Negative outlook. In the context of rising interest costs and large forward capex commitments, any sustained pivot toward private credit could signal that Oracle’s funding flexibility is eroding, highlighting the tension between its aggressive AI buildout ambitions and the limits of its investment grade balance sheet. Hardware Semiconductor providers, particularly NVIDIA and AMD, occupy a distinct but symbiotic position in the AI and hyperscale ecosystem. Their role is upstream, selling the critical compute engines that power training and inference workloads, but unlike the hyperscalers or AI model developers, they operate capital-light business models with minimal exposure to the physical data center build cycle. NVIDIA’s dominance in AI accelerators and AMD’s emerging share gains through its MI300 platform have made both indispensable suppliers to Microsoft, OpenAI, and the broader neocloud landscape, effectively monetizing the sector’s capex intensity without carrying it. While the hyperscalers commit tens of billions annually to infrastructure, NVIDIA and AMD largely outsource fabrication to TSMC and rely on design-driven innovation cycles, maintaining high incremental margins and rapid cash conversion. Going forward, even as AI infrastructure spend remains elevated, these chipmakers are unlikely to see comparable capex burdens; their investment will continue to concentrate in R&D and supply-chain alignment rather than owned capacity. In this way, they remain leveraged to AI growth through demand visibility and pricing power, but structurally insulated from the balance sheet drag faced by hyperscale cloud operators. How do securitizations fit into the data center financing ecosystem? Securitizations typically finance in-place/stabilized cashflows, meaning the market generally doesn’t do a great job of securitizing construction loans given construction risks. However, construction guarantees could open the path to construction securitizations, and so far, there has been one such deal that we know of (GSMS 2025-800D). The deal was on the smaller side at \$474mn for a single 30MW site buildout in Elk Grove Village, IL, and the mortgage loan was struck at 1m Term SOFR + 300bp, 75bp back of a mostly stabilized \~\$2bn portfolio (BX 2025-VLT6) that priced a month prior.
Instead, the CRE financing market has facilitated construction-only financings of AI factories that rival the power capacity of the recent Meta/Blue Owl transaction. Unlike the Meta/Blue Owl transaction, which rolls up construction and amortizing permanent financing into one, CRE construction loans are fully amortizing and cover only the construction period. Banks are the largest lenders and syndicators in this space. Once construction is complete, the operator may want to re-lever the asset with new financing. At 1m Term SOFR + 200-250bp for IG hyperscale tenanted built-to-suits with guaranteed leases, we think these kinds of fully amortizing construction loans offer some of the best risk/reward in the data center debt complex.
The question, of course, is whether AI data centers can be securitized as the sector's permanent financing needs grow. Private credit focus right now is finding the ‘right ‘ structure
Given the sheer scale of AI/Data Center projects, issuers have been searching for creative solutions to garner additional financing in more balance sheet efficient manners, by merging some of the features of the ABS, CMBS, Construction Finance and HG markets. This is also a reflection of public credit markets adapting to the competitive challenge of more flexible private credit markets by reintroducing structural complexity to public markets without giving up the liquidity and price discovery advantages of the public markets. The recent Beignet transaction is a marquee example of this.
Last month, Meta completed a landmark \$27.3bn private financing through Beignet Investor LLC, a vehicle arranged by Blue Owl to fund its next-generation data center build, marking one of the largest off-balance sheet transactions ever by a U.S. corporate. The structure reflects Meta’s strategic effort to finance its massive AI infrastructure program while preserving balance sheet flexibility and headline credit metrics. By partnering with private investors through an off-balance sheet JV, Meta effectively transforms what would otherwise be direct capex and on-balance sheet debt into long-term lease obligations, smoothing cash outflows and limiting reported leverage. Such structures are increasingly attractive for hyperscalers, enabling them to secure durable, fixed-rate capital at competitive terms without pressuring public debt markets or liquidity. For investors, these JVs offer exposure to high-quality tenants and stable, asset-backed cash flows, while issuers retain operational control of critical infrastructure. We expect other hyperscalers to pursue similar vehicles to diversify funding sources, reduce headline leverage, and better match financing with the longduration nature of AI data center assets.
Meta’s recent data center JV was structured through Beignet Investor LLC and involves \$27.3bn of senior secured amortizing notes maturing 2049 (RPLDCI 6.581% ‘49s) to fund Blue Owl’s 80% equity share, with Meta contributing the remaining 20% (\~\$6bn) and overseeing all construction. The debt is fully prefunded, invested in laddered Treasuries during construction, and repaid from lease payments under 20-year triple net leases between Meta’s tenant entity, Pelican Leap LLC, and the project landlord, Laidley LLC, supported by a residual-value guarantee that ensures all debt is fully repaid if leases terminate (see our note here). Meta assumes all costoverruns and delay risk and provides payment guarantees on rent, operating expenses, and termination payments, leaving bondholders primarily exposed to Meta’s credit and long-term occupancy of the site. S&P has opted not to consolidate the JV debt onto Meta’s balance sheet because Meta will only own just 20% of the equity investment and has the ability to exit the JV. Instead, the agency will adjust the company’s operating leases to account for the present value of eight years of the company’s lease payments to the JV in its adjusted debt calculation once the payments commence in 2029. We expect the agency to treat other project financing structures similarly in the future.

Research further underscores this trend: the prominence and click-through rates (CTR) of Google’s classic search links have fallen significantly due to features like “AI Overviews,” which deliver synthesized answers directly at the top of search results. These AI-generated summaries often satisfy user queries without requiring visits to external websites. According to a Pew Research Center study, users shown an AI summary were nearly half as likely to click on a traditional search result (8% CTR vs 15%). As a result, publishers and content creators who depend on organic search traffic are seeing substantial declines in visitors, with some reporting drops of 30-40%. This transformation marks a shift from Google’s role as a “referral engine” to an “answer engine,” fundamentally reshaping the digital landscape and challenging established SEO and publishing business models. The monetization of AI is thus not only a matter of internal strategy for hyperscalers but is also driving profound changes in how information is accessed and distributed online.

But if that doesn’t materialize, what happens? History as a guide
Telecommunications and the dot-com bubble. At the turn of the century, there was a boom in investment in the telecommunications space as a result of the need for a means to access the expected exponential growth in data available on the Internet. Small companies with thin balance sheets and heady business models were springing up in droves. Those companies came to be known as “dot-coms” due to their web-based sale of services, merchandise and even music. Thus, telecom carriers began to build networks that could carry the data required by these new offerings more efficiently through fiber optic networks and Internet capable wireless services.
European rush to build high-speed wireless. In 2000, European governments began auctioning off licenses for 3G wireless services with the promise of delivering new revenue streams for services that could take advantage of 3G’s “blazing” 0.4 Mbps speeds. Licenses previously had been awarded based on “beauty contests” to companies that could most readily provide good service. But the 3G auctions were highly competitive and generated record fees for countries such as the UK and Germany.

European telecom companies spent roughly \$100bn buying those licenses and then needed another \$100bn to build the new infrastructure required to take advantage of that spectrum. That may not seem like much money in the context of what we are seeing with AI spending, but the telecom companies had relatively little free cash flow. That spending strained their balance sheets and pressured their credit ratings. For example, between September 2001 and July 2002, Orange (formerly France Telecom) had its corporate credit rating downgraded three notches by Standard & Poor’s: from “A-“ to one notch above junk at “BBB-“.
Fiber optic telecom buildouts. During the same period, a number of smaller new-age telecom companies began raising significant amounts of debt to build fiber-optic networks. Those networks were far more capable of transmitting the large amounts of Internet traffic than the copper-based networks they displaced. The networks consisted of long-haul connections, both terrestrial and undersea, and local metropolitan based fiber connections. Conventional wisdom at the time said that Internet data usage was doubling every 100 days, which helped fuel the significant debt-driven investment in the business. One of the companies, Global Crossing, saw its market cap grow to over \$50bn in early 2000 with LTM revenues of only about \$1.7bn.
What went wrong? In the European wireless space, the adoption curve was much slower than the telecom companies anticipated. Wireless Internet connectivity was initially expensive for customers, and the phones required to make use of 3G were expensive too. That meant it would take far longer for the telecom companies to recoup their investments and drove the cost of debt funding higher as well.
There were several issues in the fiber-optic business that caused problems. First, there was the fallout from the failure of a significant number of financially weak dot-com companies that led to the scrutiny of the forecasts of exponential data needs of those businesses. Second, there was a bottleneck in getting data to consumers. Most homes still had copper connections, and even the fastest cable internet connections were delivering only about 1.5 Mbps. For enterprise customers, there was a slower-thanexpected adoption rate that also crimped data needs. All of that, along with advances in technology, led to a relative glut in fiber capacity that drove down prices on a unit of capacity - a trend that still exists today. Finally, many of the fiber telecom companies expanded their networks by swapping routes in areas where they had built fiber for the fiber routes of other carriers in a different geography. Because accounting standards allowed for the outward portion of the swap to be recorded as revenue and the inward half to be recorded as capex, it became a popular way for companies to grow their network footprint while increasing EBITDA.
Similarities and Differences to the data center spending today. There are several lessons we can learn from the telecom bubble. First, there were relatively large sums of money being spent without a clear understanding of how the adoption curve would play out. And it appears that is also the issue with the spending going on in AI today. It is also not clear exactly what end users, Enterprise or Consumer, will want to pay for the use of AI-based models. While the need for data center compute power may be exponentially increasing, competition and limitations on efficiency could keep revenues from following. As an example, Altice US charged \$35 per month for a 1.5Mbps connection in 1998. Today they charge only \$65 for an exponentially faster 1,000Mbps connection.

There are also some similarities in the circular nature of some of the funding of fiber-optic network builders in 2002 and the of data centers we see today. The fiber route swaps were somewhat circular in nature, and investor fear set in when they found out that the network builders were selling most of their inventory in cashless transactions to each other. Those cashless swaps eventually caught up with the weaker players in the business. Their bankruptcies followed, which then led to a collapse of the industry.
But there are differences too. The most significant of those involves the credit strength of many of the key companies that are buying data center compute power. Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft all generate an enormous amount of FCF despite spending capex at a consensus estimated level in 2025 that is roughly \$200bn higher than in 2022. Those companies are in far better financial shape than the weaker dotcoms and over-levered fiber builders were in 2002.
Rapid disruption via a step change is another risk
The problem with trying to predict disruption is that once you know what the disruption is, it’s often too late to do anything about it. The market is fully cognizant of that fact, hence the market reaction to even a hint of potential disruption. Regardless, an investment boom predicated on bringing potentially zettaflops of computing capacity that could consume 100+ GW of power is remarkably sensitive to any step change increases in efficiency. DeepSeek provides a recent example of how quickly fears of a step change in efficiency (at once touted as training efficiencies on the order of 90%) could reverberate through the marketplace.
The DeepSeek moment was a temporary cold bucket of water. In January 2025, a Chinese AI startup named DeepSeek launched its R1 reasoning model, which reportedly matched the performance of leading models like those from OpenAI but was developed at a fraction of the cost. The announcement led to a dramatic \~\$600 billion drop in Nvidia’s market valuation, as investors reconsidered the economics and competitive landscape of AI development. Deepseek made its models globally accessible, challenging the dominance of proprietary AI systems and sparking industry-wide discussions about the future of AI development and cost efficiency. The company’s rapid rise and cost-effective approach prompted questions about global tech leadership, with China positioning itself as a major force in AI despite geopolitical challenges. Subsequent analyses ultimately suggested there was some hyperbole involved in the company’s claims. Nonetheless, the DeepSeek episode serves as a cautionary tale for the risks inherent in any rapidly evolving technology space, such as artificial intelligence. It highlights how disruptive innovation can emerge unexpectedly, challenging established players and forcing entire industries to reassess their assumptions about cost, competition, and technological leadership. In fast-moving fields like AI, the risk of sudden paradigm shifts—where new entrants redefine what is possible—underscores the need for vigilance on the part of investors that seek to participate in this space.
Will smaller players build a better mousetrap? We’ve talked a lot about large hyperscalers and a little about smaller hyperscalers and OpenAI, but its also worth paying attention to some of the smaller players that focus on AI in the data center. Necessity is often the mother of invention, and smaller, nimbler companies may unlock efficiencies others miss. Conversely, if something is going wrong in the industry or the supply chain it will likely be apparent earlier in some of the smaller companies.
